leads.title: The water closet with a trapped drain
leads.why: A water seal in a bent pipe made an indoor toilet tolerable, and with sewers it became the standard fixture of homes worldwide.
leads.verify: Cumming's 1775 patent and Bramah's 1778 valve closet; Harington's 1596 design; the growth of use after 1850; the far older water-flushed latrines of the Indus cities and Minoan Crete, which another slice may cover.

history of the flush toilet Harington 1596 Indus latrines

leads.title: Disposable sanitary pads
leads.where: Birmingham, England, and Wisconsin, United States
leads.why: Cheap disposable pads replaced washed cloths and made school, work and travel easier for women during menstruation.
leads.verify: The first commercial disposable pads (Southall's, 1888; Lister's Towels, 1896) and the wartime cellulose wadding behind Kotex (1920 to 1921); when a majority of women in any country used them; the tampon of the 1930s.
search: history of menstrual products Museum of Menstruation disposable pads

leads.title: Human dissection in Italian universities
leads.why: Dissection taught in medical schools and printed with exact pictures overturned Galen's animal-based anatomy and made observation the test in medicine.
leads.verify: The earliest documented teaching dissections at Bologna (Mondino, about 1315); the 1543 publication of Vesalius's Fabrica; whether the revival knew of Alexandrian practice only through Galen.
search: Mondino de Luzzi Anathomia 1316 dissection Bologna
Park Secrets of Women origins of human dissection Italy

leads.title: Caesarean section in Bunyoro
leads.date: observed 1879; age of the practice unknown
leads.why: Healers in Bunyoro delivered by abdominal section using banana wine, cautery and pinned closure, with mother and child recovering, when the operation was still usually fatal in Europe.
leads.verify: Robert Felkin's 1884 account of the operation he watched at Kahura; any other evidence for the practice in the Great Lakes region; how historians judge its age and independence.
search: Felkin 1884 caesarean section Uganda Kahura Edinburgh Medical Journal

leads.title: Sutured caesarean section in Germany
leads.why: Stitching the womb closed, with antisepsis, made the operation survivable, and about a fifth of the world's children are now born this way.
leads.verify: Kehrer's 1881 and Sanger's 1882 operations and papers; maternal death rates before and after; earlier operations the mother survived (for example in Cape Town in 1826) and Porro's 1876 method.
search: history of caesarean section maternal mortality nineteenth century

leads.title: Positive-pressure ventilation and intensive care in Copenhagen
leads.why: Hand-ventilating polio patients through a tracheostomy halved their death rate and led straight to mechanical ventilators and the intensive care unit.
leads.verify: Bjorn Ibsen's method in the 1952 epidemic and the fall in mortality; the opening date of the first intensive care unit (1953); the earlier iron lung (1928) and the ventilators that followed.
